title: Ukang
localName: Ukang — smoked fish in scent leaf stew
author: Iquo Bassey
desc: Three whole smoked fish and three cups of finely sliced scent leaf, with the palm oil poured over the fish rather than stirred in, so nothing breaks up.
longDesc: Ukang is an Oron dish of Akwa Ibom — smoked fish in a scent leaf stew — and it is the simplest soup in this collection. Water, dry pepper, crayfish and seasoning boil for three minutes, the washed fish goes in with some of the scent leaf and the pot is shaken rather than stirred, and it cooks until the water is almost dry. The palm oil is then poured over the fish, which both coats them and avoids breaking them, and the rest of the scent leaf goes in for two or three minutes until wilted. Note the palm oil quantity is printed ambiguously and is flagged rather than resolved.
ingredients: 3 whole medium-size smoked fish — silver catfish or shiny nose
1/2 - 1 cooking spoon scotch bonnet pepper, coarsely ground
3 cups finely sliced scent leaf (ntong, efinrin, nchawun), used in two additions
Palm oil — see the note on quantity
steps: Add 2 to 3 cups of water to the pot with the dry pepper, the crayfish and the seasoning, and boil 3 minutes.
Wash the fish and add it to the pot to cook and soften.
Add some of the scent leaf and shake the pot rather than stirring.
Cook until the water is almost dry.
Add the palm oil, pouring it over the fish to prevent them breaking, and cook 1 minute.
Add the remaining scent leaf and cook 2 to 3 minutes, until wilted.
Serve with boiled yam or plantain.
chefTips: Shake the pot, do not stir. Smoked fish falls apart the moment a spoon touches it.
Pour the palm oil over the fish rather than into the liquid. It coats them and it is also the gentlest way to add it.
Until the water is almost dry is the cue before the oil goes in. This is a stew, not a soup.
Scent leaf in two additions — some early with the fish, the rest at the end. Early for depth, late for aroma.
Finely sliced scent leaf, three cups in total. The page does not say how to divide it between the two additions, so split it roughly in half.

ON THE PALM OIL: the source prints '21/2 cups', almost certainly 2 1/2 with a lost space, and adds 'you can use more or less'. Two and a half cups is a very large amount even for a palm-oil-forward Oron stew, and half a cup is also a plausible reading of the same characters. Start with half a cup and add more to taste — the ambiguity is in the source and is not resolved here.
Silver catfish or shiny nose are the fish named. Any firm smoked fish will do.
commonMistakes: Stirring the pot and breaking the fish.
Adding the oil before the water has reduced.
Putting all the scent leaf in at once.
Taking the printed palm oil quantity at face value without tasting as you go.
Over-cooking the final scent leaf past wilted.
sources: Adapted from 'How to make Ukang?', byline '1Qfoodplatter'. Headnote as printed: 'Ukang ( smoked fish in scent leaf stew) is a delicay of Oron people in Akwa Ibom state' — typo in the original. The dish is described as a traditional treat celebrated at significant occasions including funeral rites.

Quantities as printed: 3 whole medium size Smoked fish (silver cat fish or Shinny nose); 1 teaspoon dry Pepper; 1/2 – 1 cooking spoon Scotch Bonnet Pepper (coarsely ground); 3 cups finely sliced Scent leaf (Ntong/Effirin/Nchawun); '2 tables spoon' ground Crayfish, as printed; '21/2 cups Palm Oil (you can use more or less)' as printed; Seasoning cube to taste; Water. Yield not specified.

TRANSCRIPTION FLAG, NOT RESOLVED. The palm oil prints as '21/2 cups'. That is almost certainly '2 1/2' with a lost space, but 2.5 cups is a very large amount even for a palm-oil-forward stew, and the same characters could plausibly be a typo for '1/2'. The difference is material. The quantity is therefore NOT given as a number in the ingredient list above; the source's own hedge — 'you can use more or less' — plus a practical starting point are given in the tips instead, with the ambiguity stated. No figure is asserted as sourced.

SECOND MISMATCH, flagged: the 3 cups of scent leaf are split across two additions in the method with NO division given. Half and half is suggested in the tips as a practical reading, not as a sourced instruction. The same page also prints '2 tables spoon'.

Method and times as printed: add 2-3 cups water, dry pepper, crayfish, seasoning and boil 3 minutes; wash the fish, add to the pot to cook and soften, add scent leaf, shake the pot; cook until the water is almost dry; add palm oil and cook 1 minute, 'pouring over fish to prevent breaking'; add the remaining scent leaf and cook 2-3 minutes until wilted; serve with boiled yam or plantain.

ON SCENT LEAF, from Tayo Oredola, Low Carb Africa: clove basil, Ocimum gratissimum, with five names — 'Nnchanwu (Igbo), Efinrin (Yoruba), Daidoya (Hausa), Ntong (Efik), Aramogbo (Edo)'. This recipe's own parenthesis gives three of them.
ON ITS DOCUMENTATION STATUS: a prior pass listed ukang among dishes absent from the named-author record. It is documented with quantities on this page.
healthBenefits: Smoked fish is a concentrated source of protein, calcium and omega-3 fats.
Scent leaf carries aromatic oils with documented antimicrobial activity.
Red palm oil supplies carotenoids and vitamin E.
culturalNote: Ukang belongs to the Oron people of Akwa Ibom and is made for significant occasions including funeral rites, which is a reminder that the simplest dishes are not always the most casual. Three fish, three cups of a single herb and some palm oil — it is a dish that depends entirely on the quality of the smoked fish, which is exactly the kind of cooking a fishing community produces.
